title: The Bell that Came Too Late
text: Huilin's master was called Brother Mo, of the Thousand-Bowl Monastery. One spring he walked four days down from his hermitage to bless a wedding at a reed-path village called Lutaomen — he had been asked for, as monks often were, by the bride's mother, who did not trust the elder son's family. He arrived on the third evening, one evening too late. The bride was already in the water. Brother Mo rang his bell once over the reeds, for the living and for the dead, and the bell cracked on the single strike — rim to crown — as if the air itself had said *enough*. He took the bell down to the willow's roots and he gave it back to the water. He did not come home. His only disciple, a twelve-year-old named Huilin, wandered for a year looking for the sound of a bell that would not ring, and then for the rest of his life learning to be the bell that no one had struck.

title: The Tea on the Broken Bridge
text: In the forty-second year of the Silver Heron, a young sword-master from the Azure Cloud crossed the Broken Bridge carrying an old iron staff he had taken, by accident, from a monk's sleeping-mat at the Thousand-Bowl. The monk — not yet called Huilin, not yet fifty — caught him at the far end of the bridge, and they drank tea for seven hours there, from one bowl, because there was only one. The sword-master took the bowl home to Azure Cloud and kept it on the west sill of his pavilion, in a dish of river-pebbles, where he has kept it for fifty years. He will not give it back. He will not drink from it. When Huilin asks of it he says: 'Your bowl is warm. Come and sit; it will not travel further.' That is their oath. Neither of them has ever broken it — the bowl has travelled from the Broken Bridge to the west pavilion and no further; and Huilin, by not demanding it, keeps his staff empty and his beads full.

title: The Name the Wind Finally Gave
text: The wind on the plateau will name a thing if the one who asks has carried the right stone up the last ridge. This is not a metaphor; this is a method. Brother Mo took his stone up and it was heavy; the wind did not speak. His student, carrying the stone half a century later and older than his master ever was, sat at the nine incense stubs and asked the same question: *what rose the water on the night of the wedding at Lutaomen?* This time the wind answered. The answer is not a word. It is the absence of a word where a name should be, which is how the old things hide: under the shape of the wanted sound. Something under the lake-bed; something that does not approve of matches it has not been consulted in; something that still does not have a name, but has — at last — a shape. The shape is the cracked bell. Huilin came down from the plateau and said nothing for a day; and then he said, 'It is enough to know that it does not have a name. I will stop looking for one.' And he did, though the wind is still up there waiting.
